lessons.title: Negotiating the rent
lessons.goal: Negotiate the price and conditions of a flat without losing it.

tip.title: Soft openers
tip.body: Negotiation in Spanish runs on the conditional, which softens everything: ¿Habría margen para…? (would there be room to…?), ¿Sería posible…? Show interest before you push back: Me interesa, pero el precio se sale un poco de mi presupuesto. Me lo tengo que pensar buys time without saying no. Vocabulary varies: a flat is un piso in Spain and un departamento in Mexico and Argentina (apartamento in Colombia), and the building's service charges are las expensas in Argentina but los gastos de comunidad in Spain.

tip.title: Facts, not threats
tip.body: Open calmly: Me gustaría hablar de mis condiciones. Then give evidence: He asumido más responsabilidades, Gracias a mi trabajo conseguimos… In Latin America the simple past (asumí) is often used where Spain prefers the perfect (he asumido). Ask with the conditional: Creo que sería justo… An aumento de sueldo is understood everywhere; in Spain you'll also hear una subida de sueldo. If the answer is a vague Ya veremos (we'll see), keep the door open: ¿Podríamos hablar de otras opciones? and pin down a date.

lessons.title: Reaching a compromise
lessons.goal: Make offers and counter-offers and close the deal.

tip.title: Meet in the middle
tip.body: Signal a counter-offer with Le propongo una cosa or ¿Qué le parece si + present? (¿Qué le parece si lo dejamos en dos millones?). Dejar algo en… means to settle on a price. ¿Partimos la diferencia? is "shall we split the difference?" Trade, don't just give in: Podemos ajustar el plazo, pero no el precio. Close with ¡Trato hecho! (it's a deal!) and lock it in: Lo ponemos todo por escrito. In Colombia, prices in pesos often run into millions, so get used to hearing dos millones y medio.

lessons.title: Conditions & mixed conditionals
lessons.goal: Set conditions with siempre que, con tal de que, a menos que and en caso de que + subjunctive, and mix past and present in si-clauses.

tip.title: Conditions that need the subjunctive
tip.body: Si takes the indicative in the present (Si pagas hoy, te lo dejo más barato), but these conjunctions always take the subjunctive: siempre que / siempre y cuando (as long as), con tal de que (provided that), a menos que / a no ser que (unless) and en caso de que (in case, if). Te bajo el precio siempre que pagues en efectivo. If the main verb is conditional, use the imperfect subjunctive: Lo aceptaría con tal de que me pagaran más. Careful: siempre que + indicative means "whenever" (Siempre que voy, llueve). Mixed conditionals cross time: a past condition with a present result, Si hubiera aceptado la oferta, ahora viviría en Madrid; or a present situation with a past result, Si fuera más paciente, no habría perdido el trato.

story.title: El tapete de lana
story.intro: At a craft market in Oaxaca, Rosa bargains with Don Abel over a hand-woven wool rug.

lines.name: Rosa
lines.t: Buenas tardes. ¿Cuánto cuesta este tapete de lana?
lines.n: Good afternoon. How much is this wool rug?

lines.name: Don Abel
lines.t: Buenas tardes. Ese se lo dejo en tres mil pesos. Lo tejió mi familia a mano, en telar.
lines.n: Good afternoon. I'll let you have that one for three thousand pesos. My family wove it by hand, on a loom.

lines.name: Rosa
lines.t: Está precioso, pero tres mil es mucho para mí. ¿Me lo deja en dos mil?
lines.n: It's beautiful, but three thousand is a lot for me. Will you let me have it for two thousand?

lines.name: Don Abel
lines.t: Ay, no, dos mil no puedo. Nomás la lana me cuesta casi eso. Se lo dejo en dos mil seiscientos.
lines.n: Oh, no, I can't do two thousand. The wool alone costs me almost that. I'll let you have it for two thousand six hundred.

lines.name: Rosa
lines.t: Mire, me llevo también los dos cojines, siempre que me haga un buen precio por todo.
lines.n: Look, I'll take the two cushions too, as long as you give me a good price for everything.

lines.name: Don Abel
lines.t: A ver… el tapete y los dos cojines, tres mil doscientos. Y eso porque es mi primera venta del día.
lines.n: Let's see… the rug and the two cushions, three thousand two hundred. And that's only because it's my first sale of the day.

lines.name: Rosa
lines.t: ¿Lo dejamos en tres mil? Le pago en efectivo ahorita.
lines.n: Shall we say three thousand? I'll pay you in cash right now.

lines.name: Don Abel
lines.t: Ándele pues, tres mil. Con tal de que me recomiende con sus amigas.
lines.n: All right then, three thousand. As long as you recommend me to your friends.
lines.note: Mexico: ándele pues = all right then, go on.

lessons.title: Make your offer
lessons.goal: Negotiate out loud for a minute and a half: an offer, conditions, a concession and a compromise.

culture.title: Ya veremos: the indirect no
culture.body: In many Spanish-speaking settings people avoid a flat no, especially in business or with people they don't know well. Answers like Ya veremos (we'll see), Lo vamos a pensar or, in Mexico, Ahorita lo vemos can be a polite way of saying "probably not" or "not now", so listen to the tone and follow up gently with a concrete date. Bargaining is normal at many street markets and craft stalls in Mexico and other parts of Latin America, but not in supermarkets or chain stores, and in most shops in Spain prices are fixed. When you do bargain, stay friendly: a smile and a fair counter-offer usually work better than a hard line.
